key_terms.meaning: A/F = ṁ<sub>air</sub> ÷ ṁ<sub>fuel</sub> by mass; petrol stoichiometric about 14.7:1, idle about 12:1, cruise 15–16:1, full load about 12.5:1
ṁ<sub>a</sub> = C<sub>da</sub>A<sub>t</sub>√(2ρ<sub>a</sub>Δp); ṁ<sub>f</sub> = C<sub>df</sub>A<sub>f</sub>√(2ρ<sub>f</sub>(Δp − ρ<sub>f</sub>gz))
Idle, main (with compensation), power, accelerator pump and choke
Delay from start of pump delivery to nozzle opening; crank angle θ = 6Nt (N in rpm, t in s)
Diesel DI into a piston bowl; IDI into a prechamber or swirl chamber; petrol port injection is sometimes grouped as indirect
V = (πd² ÷ 4) s<sub>eff</sub>; effective stroke from port closing to helix spill
Pump and nozzle in one body at each cylinder, driven by the engine cam; no high-pressure pipe
Q = C<sub>d</sub>A t √(2(p<sub>rail</sub> − p<sub>cyl</sub>) ÷ ρ): set by open time and pressure together
Pilot, main, after and post pulses for noise, NOx, soot and after-treatment
t<sub>inj</sub> = m<sub>air</sub> ÷ (A/F × q<sub>s</sub>) + t<sub>dead</sub>
One injector at the throttle body against one per intake port
Petrol injected into the cylinder at about 50–200 bar; homogeneous or stratified charge
ΔT ≈ h<sub>fg</sub> ÷ ((A/F) c<sub>p</sub>), about 21 K for petrol at 14.7:1
ṁ = C<sub>d</sub>A√(2ρΔp)
S = 2.95 (Δp ÷ ρ<sub>a</sub>)<sup>0.25</sup> √(d t) after break-up
F = mω²r; δ = (N<sub>nl</sub> − N<sub>fl</sub>) ÷ N<sub>fl</sub>
E = ½LI²; i = (V/R)(1 − e<sup>−t/τ</sup>), τ = L/R; t<sub>dwell</sub> = dwell angle ÷ (6 × distributor rpm)

A focused nanosecond pulse breaks the gas down into a plasma; no electrodes

takeaways: A carburettor's venturi and main jet give one mixture strength; idle, power, accelerator and choke circuits add fuel where the engine's demand curve departs from it.
A fuel injection system must meter, pressurise, time, atomise and distribute the fuel; injection lag is a fixed time, so its crank angle grows with speed.
In a jerk pump the helix sets the effective stroke and so the quantity; a distributor pump does the same with one element for all cylinders.
Common rail separates pressure from timing: quantity depends on open time and rail pressure together, and split injection lowers noise, NOx and soot.
Electronic fuel injection turns measured air per cycle into a pulse width plus dead time; the oxygen sensor closes the loop near 14.7:1.
Gasoline direct injection cools the charge, allows a higher compression ratio and stratified lean running, at the cost of particulates and valve deposits.
Nozzle hole size, number and pressure trade atomisation against penetration; penetration must reach the bowl's air without wetting the wall.
A governor is a closed-loop speed controller; a mechanical governor needs some droop, while isochronous control holds one speed.
Battery-coil and magneto ignition both break a primary current to induce the spark; a fixed dwell angle weakens the battery-coil spark at high speed.
Electronic ignition controls dwell and timing without points, CDI stores energy in a capacitor, and laser ignition removes the electrodes; spark advance rises with speed and falls with load.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for labelled sketches with the working: the simple carburettor, the jerk and distributor pumps, the common rail and electronic injection layouts, the governor and the ignition circuits. Calculations on the simple carburettor, fuel per injection and plunger size are common, and recent syllabi add gasoline direct injection, electronic ignition and laser ignition.

bank.q: With a neat sketch, explain the working of a simple carburettor. Draw the mixture requirement curve of a petrol engine and explain why a practical carburettor needs idle, main, power, accelerator and choke circuits.
outline: Parts: air filter, float chamber, float and needle valve, nozzle and main jet, venturi, throttle, choke
Venturi depression lifts petrol; tip above the float level
Mixture curve: rich idle, lean cruise, rich full load, transient enrichment
Simple carburettor richens as flow rises and cannot follow the curve
Role of each circuit and when it acts
answer: Purpose: a petrol (SI) engine needs a combustible air-petrol mixture whose strength suits each operating condition. The carburettor meters petrol into the air in proportion to the air flow, atomises it and lets the throttle control how much mixture enters.

answer.text: Sketch: draw a vertical tube with the air filter at the top, the choke butterfly, a venturi (a smooth narrowing to a throat and widening again), the fuel nozzle ending in the throat, and the throttle butterfly below the venturi. Beside it draw the float chamber with the float, the needle valve at the petrol inlet, the vent, the petrol level, and the main jet at the bottom feeding the nozzle; the nozzle tip is a few millimetres above the petrol level. The figure of the simple carburettor in the carburettor chapter can be reproduced.

answer: Float chamber: the float rises with the petrol and pushes the needle onto its seat, shutting the inlet. The level, and so the head on the jet, stays constant. The chamber is vented to the air-filter side, so it is at near-atmospheric pressure.

Working: on the suction stroke air rushes through the venturi. By continuity its speed is highest at the throat, and by Bernoulli its pressure is lowest there. The difference between the float-chamber pressure and the throat pressure (the venturi depression, typically a few hundredths of a bar) pushes petrol through the main jet and out of the nozzle. The fast air stream breaks the petrol into droplets, which partly evaporate on the way to the cylinder.

Why the tip is above the level: when the engine stops there is no depression, and the 4 to 6 mm lift stops petrol from dribbling out. The fuel therefore sees Δp − ρ<sub>f</sub>gz, and no fuel flows until the depression exceeds this small head.

Air filter and throttle: the filter (dry paper, oil-bath or oiled foam) removes dust that would wear the bore and rings; a choked filter enriches the mixture. The throttle sets the quantity of mixture and so the power, since an SI engine is quantity-governed.

answer.text: Mixture requirement curve: plot A/F against load from idle to full load. Typical values:

head: Condition
A/F (by mass)
Reason
rows: low air speed, poor vaporisation, high residual-gas dilution
maximum power; extra fuel cools the charge
fuel film in the manifold lags the air
only the light fractions evaporate from cold surfaces

answer: Limit of the simple carburettor: with z neglected, A/F = (C<sub>da</sub>A<sub>t</sub> ÷ C<sub>df</sub>A<sub>f</sub>)√(ρ<sub>a</sub>/ρ<sub>f</sub>), a nearly fixed ratio; in practice the mixture gets richer as air flow rises, because the air density at the throat falls with depression and the fuel discharge coefficient rises. It is too lean (or delivers nothing) at idle and too rich at high flow, so it cannot follow the curve.

Idle circuit: with the throttle nearly shut the venturi depression is tiny, but the manifold vacuum below the throttle is high. A small passage from the float chamber opens just below the throttle edge and draws a rich mixture; an idle mixture screw sets it. A progression (transfer) port just above the throttle edge carries the engine smoothly into the main circuit.

Main circuit with compensation: from part load upward the main jet supplies petrol through the venturi. A compensating jet or an air-bleed emulsion tube admits air into the fuel well as flow rises, so the main circuit holds the lean cruise mixture instead of richening.

Power (economy) circuit: at full load the manifold vacuum falls; a vacuum piston or a metering rod lets a spring open an extra jet, enriching to about 12.5:1. At cruise the high vacuum keeps it shut for economy.

Accelerator pump: a plunger linked to the throttle squirts a short shot of petrol into the venturi when the throttle is opened quickly, filling the lean 'flat spot' while the manifold fuel film catches up.

Choke: a butterfly at the inlet, closed for cold starting. It restricts air, so the depression at the jet rises and a very rich mixture is drawn; it must be opened as the engine warms, or it washes oil from the bore and fouls plugs.

Conclusion: the venturi and main jet meter fuel in proportion to air flow for one mixture strength; the idle, power, accelerator and choke circuits add fuel where the engine's demand curve departs from that strength.

bank.q: State the requirements of a fuel injection system. Classify injection systems, and define injection timing, injection lag and injection duration with a crank-angle sketch.
outline: Meter, pressurise, time, atomise, distribute
Air and solid injection; direct and indirect; mechanical and electronic; continuous and intermittent
Timing as start of delivery; lag from pipe wave and opening pressure; duration from opening to closing
θ = 6Nt converts time to crank angle
answer: Requirements (all five are expected):

head: Requirement
Why it is needed
rows: the fuel per cycle must match load, and every cylinder must get the same amount
fuel must enter against compressed air and leave the holes fast enough to atomise
injection must start at the right crank angle for the speed and load
small droplets evaporate and mix fast; a solid jet burns late and smokes
the spray must reach the air in the chamber without wetting the wall
no dribble after the end of injection, which would give smoke and deposits

answer: Classification by method: air (air-blast) injection, where compressed air carries the fuel in, now obsolete because of its large compressor; and solid (airless) injection, where a pump pressurises the fuel and forces it through a nozzle. All modern systems are solid injection.

Classification by where fuel is injected: diesel direct injection into a bowl in the piston (in-line pump, distributor pump, unit injector, common rail); diesel indirect injection into a prechamber or swirl chamber in the head; petrol port (manifold) injection before the inlet valve, and petrol direct injection into the cylinder.

Classification by pumping arrangement (diesel): individual pump for each cylinder (in-line jerk pump), distributor pump (one element serves all cylinders), unit injector (pump and nozzle in one body), common rail (pressure stored in a rail).

Classification by control and delivery: mechanical (cam, plunger, helix) or electronic (sensors, ECU, solenoid or piezo injectors); continuous (the old mechanical petrol system with an air-flow plate) or intermittent (timed pulses, as in every diesel pump and modern injector).
Injection timing: the crank angle before TDC at which the pump begins to deliver fuel (static or spill timing). Some books define it at nozzle opening; state the definition you use.

Injection lag: the delay between the start of pump delivery and the nozzle opening. It comes from the pressure wave travelling along the pipe at about the speed of sound in diesel (near 1400 m/s), from fuel compressibility, and from the time for pressure to reach the nozzle opening pressure. It is a time, so its crank angle grows with speed: θ = 6Nt.
Injection duration: the crank angle from nozzle opening to closing, which grows with the fuel quantity.

answer.text: Sketch and numbers: draw a crank-angle line with TDC marked; mark start of delivery, nozzle opening and closing. For example, delivery at 20° before TDC, a 0.7 m pipe (0.5 ms lag) and 1.5 ms duration give:

answer: Consequence: because lag and duration are fixed times, they cover more crank degrees at higher speed, so mechanical pumps carry an automatic timing advance and electronic systems advance the start of injection with speed.
Check: 0.7 m ÷ 1400 m/s = 0.5 ms; 18° − 14° = 4° after TDC, as in the table.

bank.q: Explain, with sketches, the construction and working of an in-line jerk-type fuel injection pump and a distributor-type pump, and state how each meters and times the fuel.
outline: Cam, roller tappet, plunger and barrel, ports, helix, rack, delivery valve
Start at port closing, end when the helix uncovers the spill port
Rotating the plunger changes the effective stroke
Distributor pump: one element, rotor or cam plate, control sleeve, outlets in firing order
Timing marks and spill timing

answer.text: Jerk pump sketch: draw a barrel with an inlet port and a spill port opposite each other, the plunger inside with a vertical groove leading to a helical cut, the delivery valve and spring above, and the cam with a roller tappet below; a toothed control sleeve on the plunger meshes with the rack. The jerk pump figure (start and end of delivery) can be reproduced.

answer: Construction: one pumping element per cylinder sits in a common housing, driven by a camshaft at half engine speed on a four-stroke engine. The plunger is lapped into its barrel to a clearance of a few micrometres, so it seals without rings. A spring returns the plunger and keeps the tappet on the cam.
Filling: with the plunger at the bottom, diesel from the gallery (fed by a feed pump at a few bar) fills the barrel through both ports.

Start of delivery: the cam lifts the plunger. When its top edge covers both ports the fuel is trapped; pressure rises, opens the light delivery valve and travels along the pipe until the nozzle opens at its set pressure.

End of delivery: as the plunger rises further, the helix reaches the spill port. The space above the plunger now connects through the vertical groove to the spill port, pressure collapses and delivery ends; the rest of the stroke only pushes fuel back to the gallery.

Metering: the rack turns the plunger. This moves the helix relative to the spill port, so spill comes earlier or later; the effective stroke changes while the total cam lift stays the same. Volume per injection V = (πd² ÷ 4)s<sub>eff</sub>: for d = 8 mm and s<sub>eff</sub> = 3 mm, V = 50.27 × 3 = 150.8 mm³. With the vertical groove facing the spill port there is no effective stroke: the stop position.

Delivery valve: its retraction piston draws back a small volume of fuel as it closes, so line pressure drops sharply and the nozzle snaps shut without dribble, while a residual pressure keeps the pipe primed.

answer.text: Distributor pump (axial-plunger type) sketch: one plunger driven by a cam plate with as many lobes as cylinders, riding on fixed rollers; a distributor slot in the plunger; a control sleeve moved by the governor; outlets to each injector around the head.

answer: Working: the cam plate makes the plunger reciprocate and rotate together. Each lobe gives one pumping stroke, and the rotation lines up the distributor slot with the outlet of the cylinder due to fire, in firing order. Delivery ends when the plunger's spill port leaves the control sleeve; moving the sleeve changes the effective stroke and so the quantity. In the radial-plunger type, opposed plungers in a rotor are driven inward by an internal cam ring and quantity is set by inlet metering.

answer.text: Comparison:

answer: Timing: for static (spill) timing, cylinder one is set to the specified angle before TDC on compression, the delivery valve is removed and the pump is turned until fuel just stops spilling from that outlet (port closing); marks on the pump flange and flywheel are then aligned. Dynamic timing is checked with a timing light with the engine running.
Check: π × 8² ÷ 4 = 50.27 mm²; × 3 mm = 150.8 mm³ per stroke, matching the worked example.

bank.q: With a layout sketch, describe a common rail direct injection system. Explain how rail pressure, injection timing and quantity are controlled independently, and the purpose of pilot, main and post injection.
outline: Tank, lift pump, filter, high-pressure pump, rail, pressure sensor, pressure control valve, injectors, ECU
Rail as accumulator; pressure held by closed loop
Timing and quantity from the injector pulse; Q ∝ t√Δp
Pilot, main, post: noise, NOx, soot, after-treatment
Merits and limits

answer.text: Layout sketch: fuel tank → electric lift pump → fine filter → engine-driven high-pressure pump → common rail (a thick forged tube) → short pipes to one injector per cylinder. On the rail: a pressure sensor and a pressure control (or limiting) valve with a return to the tank. An ECU receives rail pressure, speed, crank and cam position, accelerator position, air mass and coolant temperature, and drives the pressure valve and each injector. The common rail figure can be reproduced.

answer: Low-pressure side: the lift pump supplies diesel at a few bar through a fine filter. Filtration matters because the pump and injector clearances are a few micrometres.

Pressure generation: the high-pressure pump runs continuously and fills the rail; the rail's volume damps the pulses, so every injector sees the same, steady pressure, typically 1000 to 2000 bar and above 2000 bar in newer systems.

Pressure control: the ECU compares the sensor reading with the value in its map for the present speed and load and adjusts the pressure control valve (or the pump's inlet metering valve). This closed loop sets rail pressure without reference to the injection event.
Timing control: the ECU decides the crank angle at which to energise each injector, from the crank and cam signals. Unlike a jerk pump, the start of injection is not tied to a cam profile.

Quantity control: the injector delivers Q = C<sub>d</sub>A t √(2(p<sub>rail</sub> − p<sub>cyl</sub>)/ρ). The ECU knows p<sub>rail</sub> and sets the open time t. Example: 1.0 ms at 1200 bar (cylinder 60 bar) gives 30 mm³; at 1800 bar the same 30 mm³ needs t = 1.0 × √(1140/1740) = 0.81 ms.

Injector: a solenoid or piezo actuator opens a small control valve; the pressure above the needle falls, and rail pressure under the needle lifts it. Closing the valve restores the pressure above and shuts the needle. Piezo injectors switch faster and allow closely spaced pulses.

answer.text: Split (multiple) injection:

head: Pulse
When
Purpose
rows: a few degrees before the main
burns a little fuel, shortens the delay of the main charge, lowers the rate of pressure rise and noise
carries most of the fuel, so its combustion gives most of the work
raises late-cycle temperature to burn soot
unburnt fuel heats the catalyst or regenerates the particulate filter

answer: Benefits: high pressure at all speeds, so fine sprays even at idle and low speed; independent timing; split injection that cuts noise and the NOx-soot trade-off; easy calibration for cold start and altitude; on-board diagnosis.
Limits: expensive pump, injectors and ECU; very clean fuel needed; the pump absorbs engine power; a sensor or wiring fault can stop the engine; service needs diagnostic tools.

bank.q: With circuit diagrams, explain battery-coil and magneto ignition systems, and compare them on energy source, starting, high-speed performance, maintenance and application.
outline: Battery, switch, primary, contact breaker, condenser, secondary, distributor, plugs
Collapse of primary field induces high secondary voltage; E = ½LI²
Magneto: rotating magnet induces its own primary current
Dwell time falls with speed in battery ignition; magneto output rises with speed
Comparison table

answer.text: Battery-coil circuit: 12 V battery → ignition switch → coil primary (a few hundred turns of thick wire) → contact breaker to earth, with a condenser across the points; the secondary (about a hundred times as many fine turns on the same iron core) → distributor rotor → plug leads → plugs to earth. A cam on the distributor shaft, at half crank speed, opens the points. The battery-coil figure can be reproduced.

answer: Working, points closed: primary current rises along i = (V/R)(1 − e<sup>−t/τ</sup>), τ = L/R, and stores energy E = ½LI² in the core's field. For L = 6 mH, R = 3 Ω on 12 V: full current 4 A and E = 0.5 × 0.006 × 16 = 48 mJ.

Working, points open: the primary current falls quickly; the condenser takes the current for an instant so the points do not arc and the collapse is fast. The collapsing flux links the secondary and induces 15 to 30 kV, enough to break down the plug gap. The rotor directs it to the cylinder due to fire, in firing order.

Magneto: in the rotating-magnet type a permanent magnet driven by the engine turns past a fixed core carrying the primary and secondary. The flux change induces current in the primary; the contact breaker opens at the moment of maximum primary current, and the secondary gives the spark. A condenser and, on multi-cylinder engines, a distributor are used as before. No battery is needed.

Speed effect, battery ignition: dwell is a fixed cam angle, so the closed time falls with speed. With 54° dwell on a 4-lobe cam, t = 54/(6 × distributor rpm): 6 ms at 3000 engine rpm gives i = 4(1 − e<sup>−3</sup>) = 3.80 A and 43.3 mJ; 3 ms at 6000 rpm gives 3.11 A and only 29.0 mJ.

Speed effect, magneto: the induced primary current grows with the rate of flux change, so the spark is weak at cranking speed (an impulse coupling flicks the magnet past the firing point) and strong at high speed.

answer.text: Comparison:

head: Feature
Battery-coil
Magneto
rows: good spark at low cranking speed if the battery is charged
spark weakens as dwell time falls
cheap where a battery exists anyway
two-wheelers, mowers, chainsaws, aircraft piston engines

answer: Conclusion: both rely on breaking a primary current to induce a high secondary voltage; the battery system suits vehicles that already carry a battery, the magneto suits small or safety-critical engines that must run without one.
Check: 0.5 × 0.006 × 3.80² = 0.0433 J; 0.5 × 0.006 × 3.11² = 0.0290 J; the ratio 0.67 shows a one-third fall from 3000 to 6000 rpm.

bank.q: Explain the working of a breakerless (transistorised) electronic ignition system and a capacitor discharge ignition system. Outline the basics, merits and limits of laser ignition.
outline: Drawbacks of points; TAC
Trigger types: magnetic pulse, Hall, optical
Module switches the coil; dwell and current control; DIS and coil-on-plug
CDI: capacitor charged to a few hundred volts, thyristor, E = ½CV², fast rise, short spark
Laser: focused pulse, plasma breakdown, no electrodes; window fouling and cost
answer: Why electronic ignition: contact points burn and pit, the rubbing block wears so the gap and timing drift, the current they can switch is limited, and the spark weakens at high speed. Transistor-assisted contact ignition first let the points carry only a transistor's base current; breakerless systems remove the points entirely.

answer.text: Breakerless system, block sketch: trigger in the distributor or at the crank → ignition module (power transistor and its control) → coil primary; coil secondary → distributor or directly to the plugs. The breakerless and laser ignition figure can be reproduced.

answer: Triggers: a magnetic pulse generator (toothed reluctor passing a pickup coil, giving an alternating voltage whose zero crossing marks the firing point); a Hall-effect sensor (a vane passing between a magnet and a Hall chip, giving a square wave that also works at zero speed); or an optical slotted disc.

Sequence: the trigger signal reaches the module; the module switches the transistor on and primary current builds; at the firing point it switches the transistor off; the field collapses and the secondary fires the plug.

Dwell and current control: the module switches on earlier as speed rises, so the coil current always reaches its limit before the break, and limits the current at low speed to protect the coil. This keeps the spark energy nearly constant, removing the main weakness of points ignition.

Distributorless forms: wasted-spark ignition uses one double-ended coil per pair of cylinders (1 and 4, 2 and 3), firing both plugs, one at the end of compression and one at the end of exhaust; at 3000 rpm each coil fires 50 times a second. Coil-on-plug ignition gives each plug its own coil and lets the ECU time each cylinder.

Capacitor discharge ignition: a converter charges a capacitor to a few hundred volts; the trigger fires a thyristor, which dumps the charge into the coil primary; the coil acts as a step-up transformer. E = ½CV²: 1 μF at 400 V stores 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ × 160 000 = 80 mJ, almost three times the 29 mJ of a points coil at 6000 rpm. For a four-cylinder four-stroke at 6000 rpm, 200 sparks a second need an average charging power of 200 × 0.080 = 16 W.

CDI merits and limits: very fast voltage rise (microseconds), so it fires fouled plugs and holds its energy at high speed; but the spark lasts only about a tenth of a millisecond, which is poor for lean mixtures. It suits two-wheelers, outboards and small engines.

Laser ignition basics: a nanosecond-pulse laser beam passes through a window in the head and a lens focuses it to a tiny spot. The intensity there ionises the gas into a plasma, which heats the mixture and starts a flame kernel. For 30 mJ in 6 ns, peak power is 0.030/(6 × 10⁻⁹) = 5 MW; over a 50 μm spot (area 1.96 × 10⁻⁵ cm²) the intensity is 2.5 × 10¹¹ W/cm².

Laser merits: no electrodes to erode or to quench the young flame; the ignition point can be placed in the best part of the chamber, or split into several points; breakdown gets easier at high pressure, so it suits high boost and lean mixtures; precise timing.
Laser limits: deposits foul the window, the optics must survive heat and vibration, and the laser is costly and bulky; it is used in research engines, not production vehicles.

bank.q: A simple carburettor supplies 9 kg/h of petrol at A/F = 14 to an engine. Air is at 1 bar and 30 °C; the throat depression is 0.08 bar. The nozzle tip is 6 mm above the float level. Take C<sub>da</sub> = 0.82, C<sub>df</sub> = 0.65, petrol density 740 kg/m³ and R = 287 J/kg K, and treat air as incompressible. Find (a) the throat diameter, (b) the fuel jet diameter, (c) the smallest depression at which petrol starts to flow, and comment on idling.
outline: Mass flows from fuel rate and A/F
Air density from p/RT
Throat speed and area from Bernoulli with C<sub>da</sub>
Fuel sees Δp − ρ<sub>f</sub>gz
Jet area and diameter
Start of flow when Δp = ρ<sub>f</sub>gz; idle needs its own circuit

answer.text: Data and mass flows:
Air density at inlet:
Throat: Bernoulli from the inlet (speed ≈ 0) to the throat gives the ideal speed; the discharge coefficient corrects the flow.
Fuel jet: the fuel must be lifted 6 mm, so it sees less than Δp.
(c) Start of fuel flow: petrol leaves the nozzle only when the depression exceeds the lift head.

answer: Comment: below about 0.0026 kg/s of air, roughly 7 % of the design air flow, the main nozzle gives no petrol at all, and just above it the mixture is very lean. Idling needs much less air than this with the throttle almost shut, so a separate idle circuit, drawing from the high manifold vacuum below the throttle, is essential.

Why the mixture would change with load: if the depression were raised to 0.16 bar, the air flow would rise by √2 to about 0.049 kg/s in this incompressible model, and the fuel flow by √((16000 − 43.6)/(8000 − 43.6)) = 1.416, so A/F stays near 14 at high flow but leans sharply as the depression approaches 43.6 Pa. In a real carburettor the falling air density at the throat makes the mixture richer as flow rises, which is why a compensating jet or air bleed is fitted.
Effect of neglecting z: with Δp<sub>f</sub> = 8000 Pa, C<sub>f</sub> = 4.650 m/s and d<sub>f</sub> = 1.194 mm, a difference of only 0.1 %, so z matters at low flow but hardly at design flow.
Answer: (a) throat diameter about 20.0 mm; (b) jet diameter about 1.20 mm; (c) about 43.6 Pa, so the main circuit cannot serve idling.

bank.q: A four-cylinder petrol engine is converted from a carburettor to sequential multi-point fuel injection. Describe the sensors, ECU and fuel system needed, with a layout sketch. If each cylinder draws 0.28 g of air per cycle at 4000 rpm, the target A/F is 14.7 and each injector flows 2.2 g/s with 0.9 ms dead time, find the pulse width and the duty cycle; repeat the duty at 6500 rpm.
outline: Fuel system: pump, filter, rail, regulator, injectors at the ports
Sensors: air flow or MAP, throttle, coolant and air temperature, crank, cam, oxygen
ECU: air per cycle → fuel → pulse width + dead time; open and closed loop
Calculation of pulse and duty
Benefits over the carburettor

answer.text: Layout sketch: air filter → air-flow sensor → throttle body with throttle position sensor → intake manifold → one injector per port aimed at the inlet valve; tank pump → filter → fuel rail with pressure regulator (about 3 bar) → injectors; ECU with sensor inputs and injector outputs. The multi-point injection figure can be reproduced.

answer: Fuel system to add: an electric in-tank pump (higher pressure than a carburettor's mechanical pump), a fine filter, a fuel rail, a pressure regulator that holds a fixed pressure across the injectors and returns the excess, and four solenoid injectors in the intake ports. The carburettor is replaced by a throttle body with an idle air control.

answer.text: Sensors and why each is needed:

head: Sensor
Measures
Used for
rows: air mass per unit time (or density)
pedal demand, idle and full throttle
acceleration enrichment, full-load enrichment, fuel cut
when to inject; air per cycle

answer: ECU strategy: it estimates the air per cylinder per cycle, divides by the target A/F to get the fuel mass, divides by the injector's static flow to get the open time, adds the dead time, and applies corrections (cold start, acceleration, battery voltage). In closed loop the oxygen sensor trims the pulse; at cold start and wide-open throttle it runs open loop from tables.

answer.text: Calculation at 4000 rpm:
answer.pre:
fuel per cylinder per cycle = 0.28 ÷ 14.7 = 0.019 05 g
fuel time = 0.019 05 ÷ 2.2 = 0.008 658 s = 8.66 ms
pulse width = 8.66 + 0.9 = 9.56 ms
cycle time = 2 rev × 60 ÷ 4000 = 0.030 s = 30 ms
duty = 9.56 ÷ 30 = 0.319, about 32 %

answer.text: At 6500 rpm with the same air charge:
answer.pre:
pulse width = 9.56 ms (unchanged)
cycle time = 120 ÷ 6500 = 0.018 46 s = 18.46 ms
duty = 9.56 ÷ 18.46 = 0.518, about 52 %

answer: Interpretation: the duty must stay well below 100 % (designers aim for about 80 % at peak power) or the injector cannot finish one pulse before the next; 52 % leaves margin. If the duty were too high, larger injectors or higher fuel pressure would be needed.

Benefits of the conversion: accurate fuel in each cylinder, closed-loop control that lets a three-way catalyst work, better cold start and transient response, fuel cut on overrun, an air-only manifold that can be tuned for breathing, and lower emissions.

bank.q: A direct-injection diesel nozzle has 6 holes of 0.18 mm diameter, C<sub>d</sub> = 0.68. The injection pressure is 950 bar and the cylinder pressure 50 bar; diesel density 830 kg/m³ and cylinder air density 25 kg/m³. Find the fuel flow, the fuel injected in 1.2 ms, the jet speed and the spray penetration 0.6 ms after the start of injection. Explain how hole size, hole number and pressure affect atomisation, penetration and cone angle, and how you would choose the nozzle for a deep bowl of 40 mm radius.
outline: Area of holes; ṁ = C<sub>d</sub>A√(2ρΔp)
Fuel per injection and jet speed
Break-up time and penetration from the correlation
Effects of hole size, number, pressure and air density
Match penetration to bowl; avoid wall wetting

answer.text: Flow area:
Mass flow:
Fuel per injection and jet speed:
Penetration (Hiroyasu–Arai): first check that the jet has broken up.

answer: Hole size: smaller holes give smaller droplets (lower Sauter mean diameter) and shorter penetration (S ∝ √d), but less flow per hole, so injection lasts longer unless more holes are used.

Hole number: at the same total area, more holes mean smaller holes, finer sprays, and jets that each reach less far; jets can also be aimed at more of the bowl's air. Too many holes in a small bowl make the jets merge and starve each other of air.

Pressure: higher injection pressure raises jet speed (∝ √Δp) and gives finer atomisation; penetration grows only as Δp<sup>0.25</sup>. Higher air density (turbocharging) shortens penetration and widens the cone angle of each jet.
Cone angle: the angle of each single jet, usually 10° to 25°, set mainly by hole geometry (length-to-diameter ratio, inlet rounding) and widened by denser air.

Choice for a 40 mm bowl: at 0.6 ms the tips reach 42 mm, just past the 40 mm wall, so liquid would wet the wall at full load, giving smoke and oil dilution. Options: use 7 or 8 holes of about 0.16 mm (S falls in proportion to √d: 42 × √(0.16/0.18) = 39.6 mm), reduce full-load injection pressure, or increase swirl to bend the jets; choose a VCO nozzle to remove the sac and its dribble.
Check: 0.0401 × 0.0012 = 4.82 × 10⁻⁵ kg = 48.2 mg; 3.6 × 10⁶ to the power 0.25 = 43.56; the break-up time 0.09 ms is far shorter than 0.6 ms, so the second formula applies.

bank.q: Explain, with a sketch, how a mechanical centrifugal governor holds the speed of a diesel generator set when load is suddenly removed. Each flyball has a mass of 0.2 kg; at full load the set runs at 1500 rpm with a ball path radius of 60 mm, and at no load at 1560 rpm with a radius of 66 mm. Find the droop and the centrifugal force on one ball at both conditions, and explain the effect of the spring stiffness and of the pneumatic type.
outline: Spindle, flyballs, sleeve, spring, lever, rack
Load removed → speed rises → balls out → sleeve lifts → rack to less fuel → new balance
Droop = (N<sub>nl</sub> − N<sub>fl</sub>)/N<sub>fl</sub>
F = mω²r at both points
Spring rate: stiffer gives more droop and stability, softer less droop but hunting; pneumatic governor

answer.text: Sketch: a vertical spindle geared to the pump camshaft carries two flyballs on hinged arms; links from the balls lift a sleeve against a spring; a lever pivoted on the casing joins the sleeve to the fuel rack. The governor figure can be reproduced.

answer: Why a diesel needs it: there is no throttle; each cycle takes nearly the same air, and power is set by fuel alone. If load is thrown off with the rack unchanged, the surplus fuel accelerates the engine towards a dangerous over-speed.

Sequence when load is removed: speed rises → centrifugal force on the balls rises with ω² → the balls fly out → the sleeve lifts and compresses the spring → the lever pulls the rack towards less fuel → the engine's torque falls to match the small load → a new balance is reached at a slightly higher speed and larger ball radius.

answer.text: Droop:
Forces:

answer: Interpretation: a 4 % speed rise raises ω² by 8.2 %, and the larger radius adds 10 %, so the outward force rises by 19 % (352.3/296.1 = 1.19). The spring must be compressed further to balance this; that extra compression is the sleeve lift that moved the rack.

Why there is droop: a spring force changes only if the spring is compressed more, so a different rack position needs a different balance radius and therefore a different speed. A simple mechanical governor cannot hold exactly the same speed at all loads.

Spring stiffness: a stiffer spring needs a larger force change, hence a larger speed change, for the same sleeve lift: more droop but a more stable, less sensitive governor. A softer spring gives less droop and a more sensitive governor, but too soft a spring makes it overshoot and hunt (speed oscillates about the set value). Friction and linkage play add a dead band.

Pneumatic governor: a butterfly valve in a venturi of the intake, set by the accelerator, creates a depression that rises with engine speed. The depression acts on a diaphragm against a spring, and the diaphragm moves the rack. If speed rises the depression grows and the rack moves to less fuel. It is simple and cheap and suits small diesels; it is sensitive to air-filter choking and less precise than the centrifugal type.

Isochronous control: an electronic or hydraulic governor with integral action can return to exactly the set speed (zero droop), which suits a single generator; parallel sets keep some droop so they share load.
Answer: droop 4.0 %; force 296.1 N at full load and 352.3 N at no load per ball.

bank.q: Explain why spark advance must change with speed and load, and how centrifugal and vacuum advance mechanisms and an ECU map provide it. At 2400 rpm the spark-to-peak time is 3.2 ms and at 4800 rpm turbulence cuts it to 2.0 ms; peak pressure should be 15° after TDC. Find the advance at both speeds and the advance the centrifugal mechanism must add between them.
outline: Peak pressure near 10–15° after TDC; θ = 6Nt<sub>b</sub> − θ<sub>pk</sub>
Speed: burn time covers more degrees; turbulence shortens it
Load: part load diluted and slow (more advance); full load dense and knock-prone (less)
Centrifugal weights, vacuum diaphragm, ECU map and knock sensor
Calculation
answer: Purpose: the spark must start the burn early enough that peak cylinder pressure falls about 10° to 15° after TDC (MBT timing). Too early: pressure peaks before TDC, negative work, knock. Too late: pressure peaks well after TDC, power falls, fuel use and exhaust temperature rise.

Speed effect: the burn takes a time t<sub>b</sub>; the crank turns 6N degrees per second, so the burn covers 6Nt<sub>b</sub> degrees. As speed rises this angle grows, so the spark must move earlier. Turbulence rises with speed and shortens t<sub>b</sub>, so the advance rises less than in proportion.

answer.text: Calculation:

answer: Check: if the burn time had stayed 3.2 ms at 4800 rpm, the burn would cover 92.2° and need 77.2° advance, which is impossible; real engines rely on turbulence.

Load effect: at part load the throttled charge has low density and a high share of residual exhaust gas, so it burns slowly and needs more advance. At full load the charge is dense and hot and the end gas is near auto-ignition, so less advance is used to avoid knock.

Centrifugal advance: two weights on the distributor shaft fly out against springs as speed rises and turn the cam (or reluctor) ahead of the shaft, adding advance with speed up to a stop; the spring rates shape the curve.

Vacuum advance: a diaphragm unit, connected to a port just above the throttle, turns the breaker (or pickup) plate against the distributor's rotation at part load, when the vacuum is high. At idle the port is above a closed throttle and at full throttle the vacuum is low, so it adds nothing there.

ECU map: modern engines store advance against speed and load (manifold pressure or air flow) and correct it for coolant and intake air temperature. A knock sensor on the block detects knock; the ECU retards that cylinder a few degrees and then advances back slowly, so the engine runs close to the knock limit.

Base timing check: warm engine at specified idle, vacuum hose plugged if specified, timing light on number one lead, read the crank-pulley mark against the pointer, and turn the distributor to correct it.
Answer: about 31° at 2400 rpm and 43° at 4800 rpm; the centrifugal mechanism adds about 11.5° between them.

bank.q: With a layout sketch, explain a gasoline direct injection system and its homogeneous and stratified modes. A GDI engine injects during the intake stroke at A/F 14.7 into air that would otherwise be at 330 K; take latent heat 305 kJ/kg and c<sub>p</sub> 1.005 kJ/kg K. Estimate the charge cooling and the gain in trapped air. In stratified mode at 2500 rpm a cylinder needs 10 mg at 9 mg/ms; find the injection angle. State the merits and problems of GDI.
outline: Two-stage fuel system: tank pump, cam-driven high-pressure pump, rail, sensor, injectors in the chamber
Homogeneous: intake-stroke injection, uniform; stratified: late compression, rich cloud at the plug
Wall-, air- and spray-guided
Charge-cooling and injection-angle calculations
Merits and problems

answer.text: Layout sketch: tank pump (3 to 6 bar) → cam-driven single-plunger high-pressure pump with a quantity control valve → rail with pressure sensor and limiting valve (about 50 to 200 bar, up to 350 bar in newer systems) → one injector per cylinder with its tip in the chamber, near the spark plug; ECU controlling pump valve, injectors and spark. The GDI figure can be reproduced.

answer: Homogeneous mode: fuel is injected early in the intake stroke and has the intake and compression strokes to mix, giving a uniform near-stoichiometric charge; used at medium and full load; the three-way catalyst works normally.

Stratified mode: fuel is injected late in the compression stroke; a rich, ignitable cloud forms around the plug while the rest of the cylinder holds air, so the overall mixture is lean and the throttle can stay open, cutting pumping loss at light load. The cloud is steered by the piston bowl (wall-guided), by tumble or swirl (air-guided), or by placing the injector next to the plug (spray-guided).

answer.text: Charge cooling:
answer.pre:
fuel per kg air = 1 ÷ 14.7 = 0.0680 kg
heat absorbed = 0.0680 × 305 = 20.75 kJ per kg air
ΔT = 20.75 ÷ 1.005 = 20.6 K
charge temperature = 330 − 20.6 = 309.4 K
air mass ratio (same p) = 330 ÷ 309.4 = 1.067, about 6.7 % more air

answer: Meaning: this is an upper limit, since some heat still comes from the walls. The cooler charge is also less prone to knock, which allows about one ratio more compression, for example 10 to 11.

answer.text: Stratified injection angle:

answer: So if injection must end 40° before TDC, it starts about 57° before TDC, and the cloud has only about 40° (2.7 ms) to form, which is why high pressure and a precise spray are needed.

Merits: charge cooling and higher compression ratio, better volumetric efficiency, quicker transient response with no port wall film, less cold-start enrichment, lower pumping loss in stratified operation, precise control of fuel in each cylinder.

Problems: particulate emissions from fuel wetting the piston and liner (gasoline particulate filters are fitted), carbon deposits on the inlet valves because no fuel washes them, injector tip deposits, NOx from lean operation needing a lean NOx trap, oil dilution, high-pressure pump cost and noise, and low-speed pre-ignition in downsized turbo engines.

bank.q: A four-cylinder four-stroke diesel engine develops 60 kW at 2400 rpm with a specific fuel consumption of 0.24 kg/kWh. Diesel density is 830 kg/m³. Its in-line jerk pump has an effective stroke of 2.5 mm at full load. Find the fuel per injection in mg and mm³ and the plunger diameter. If the high-pressure pipe is 0.6 m long and the pressure wave travels at 1400 m/s, find the injection lag in crank degrees at 2400 rpm and say how the pump timing must change.
outline: Fuel per hour from power and sfc
Injections per hour for a four-stroke engine
Mass and volume per injection
Plunger area and diameter from V = (πd²/4)s<sub>eff</sub>
Lag time = length/wave speed; θ = 6Nt; timing advance

answer.text: Fuel rate:
Number of injections: each cylinder injects once every two revolutions.
answer.pre:
per cylinder per minute = 2400 ÷ 2 = 1200
all cylinders per hour = 4 × 1200 × 60 = 288 000

answer.text: Fuel per injection:
Plunger size:
Rack setting at light load: the same plunger gives less fuel by a shorter effective stroke. If the engine needs 8 mg per injection at idle:

answer: So the rack turns the plunger until the helix uncovers the spill port only 0.40 mm after port closing, against 2.5 mm at full load; the total cam lift is unchanged. The pump camshaft turns at 2400 ÷ 2 = 1200 rpm, and each element makes 1200 strokes a minute.

In practice the designer allows for leakage past the plunger and for fuel compressed in the pipe, so the next standard size up (for example 6 mm) would be chosen, with the rack setting the effective stroke.

answer.text: Injection lag:

answer: Timing: the nozzle opens about 6° after the pump starts delivery at 2400 rpm. At 1200 rpm the same lag is only 3.1°, so a fixed pump timing would inject relatively later at high speed. The pump is therefore given an automatic advance coupling (centrifugal weights between the drive and the pump camshaft) that moves the start of delivery earlier as speed rises, and the static timing is set with the expected lag in mind.

Effect of a long pipe: the lag grows in proportion to pipe length, so all pipes are made the same length to give every cylinder the same lag; this is one reason unit injectors and common rails, with short or no pipes, time more precisely.
Answer: 50 mg (60.2 mm³) per injection, plunger about 5.5 mm, lag about 6.2° at 2400 rpm.

bank.q: A diesel truck with an in-line pump gives black smoke under load and its speed hunts at idle. Trace the possible faults through the air supply, the pump and rack, the governor and the nozzles, and justify each check you would make and its order.
outline: Black smoke = too much fuel for the air, or poor mixing
Air side: filter, turbo, intake leaks
Pump: maximum-fuel stop, rack setting, timing, delivery valves, element wear
Governor: flyweights, spring, linkage play, oil; hunting from dead band or wrong spring
Nozzles: pop, spray and leak tests; sac dribble
Order from cheapest and least invasive
answer: Read the symptoms: black smoke means fuel is burning without enough air nearby: either too much fuel for the air, or fuel that does not mix (coarse spray, late injection, wall wetting). Hunting at idle means the speed-control loop has too much gain, a dead band, or an uneven fuel supply between cylinders. One fault can cause both: an uneven or dribbling cylinder makes smoke and an unsteady idle.

Check 1, air supply (quick, no tools): inspect the air filter element and its restriction indicator, the intake hoses and, if turbocharged, the boost. A choked filter starves the engine of air and gives black smoke at load; it does not explain hunting by itself.

Check 2, fuel quality and low-pressure side: water or dirt in the fuel, a clogged feed filter or air in the lines gives uneven delivery and an unsteady idle. Bleed the system and change filters; this is cheap and often cures hunting.

Check 3, injection timing: check spill or static timing against the marks. Retarded timing makes injection late, combustion runs into the expansion stroke and black smoke rises; it also lowers idle stability. Advanced timing gives knock rather than smoke.

Check 4, nozzles (remove and test on a pop tester): opening pressure against the specification (a weak spring opens early and gives a coarse spray), spray pattern from every hole (a blocked hole sends more fuel through the others and wets the wall), leak-down 10 to 20 bar below opening (a leaking seat dribbles after injection: smoke and hydrocarbons), and chatter (a sticking needle). A single bad nozzle also gives a rough, hunting idle because that cylinder fires unevenly.

Check 5, rack and maximum-fuel stop: if the full-load stop has been moved to gain power, or the rack sticks towards more fuel, the engine is over-fuelled at load and smokes. Check that the rack moves freely over its whole travel and that the stop is at the sealed setting.

Check 6, governor: at idle the governor alone holds speed. Worn flyweight pivots, a weak or wrong idle spring, low or dirty oil in the governor housing, and play in the rack linkage all create a dead band: the governor does not respond until the speed error is large, then over-corrects, and the speed oscillates (hunting). Too soft a spring makes it too sensitive and also hunts.

Check 7, pump on a test bench (most invasive, last): calibration of delivery from each element at idle and full load, delivery valve sealing and element wear. Unequal delivery between elements gives smoke from the over-fuelled cylinders and an uneven idle.

answer.text: Summary of the trace:

head: Area
Fault
Smoke
Hunting
Check
rows: dribble, low opening pressure, blocked hole

answer: Order and justification: start with the checks that are quick, cheap and need no dismantling (air filter, fuel filters and bleeding, timing marks), then remove and test the nozzles, which are the commonest cause of both symptoms, then inspect the rack and governor, and send the pump to a bench last because it is the most costly step.

Conclusion: the most likely single cause of both symptoms is a faulty nozzle or uneven element delivery; a worn governor or linkage explains hunting alone, and a choked filter, retarded timing or a moved stop explains smoke alone. Confirm by a smoke reading and a stable idle after each repair.

bank.q: Compare a carburettor, multi-point fuel injection and gasoline direct injection for metering accuracy, cylinder-to-cylinder distribution, part-load efficiency, emissions and cost, and recommend one for a 1.2-litre car that must meet current emission limits.
outline: Metering method of each
Distribution: manifold film versus port injection versus in-cylinder
Part load: throttling, stratified lean operation, charge cooling
Emissions: closed loop and catalyst; GDI particulates
Cost and complexity; justified choice
answer: Metering: a carburettor meters by venturi depression with fixed jets, so its A/F drifts with air density, temperature and wear, and it has no feedback. MPFI meters by injector pulse width at fixed pressure, with an oxygen sensor closing the loop, so it holds A/F within a narrow band around 14.7:1. GDI meters the same way but at 50 to 200 bar, and can also choose when in the cycle the fuel arrives.

Distribution: with a carburettor the fuel travels through the manifold partly as liquid film, so cylinders near and far from it get different mixtures, worst when cold. MPFI puts an injector at each port, so each cylinder gets its own measured fuel; some film still forms on the port and valve. GDI injects into each cylinder, so distribution is exact and there is no port film.

Part-load efficiency: carburettor and MPFI engines are throttled at part load and lose pumping work; MPFI can run slightly leaner and cut fuel on overrun. GDI in stratified mode can run unthrottled and lean at light load, and its charge cooling allows about one ratio more compression, both of which raise efficiency.

Emissions: a carburettor cannot hold A/F tightly enough for a three-way catalyst, so it cannot meet current limits. MPFI with closed loop and a three-way catalyst is the established low-emission solution. GDI meets the gaseous limits in homogeneous mode, but produces more particulates (usually needing a gasoline particulate filter) and, if run lean, NOx that needs a lean NOx trap.

Transient response and cold start: carburettor needs an accelerator pump and choke; MPFI handles both by pulse corrections; GDI is fastest, with no wall film, and can use split injection to heat the catalyst.

answer.text: Summary:

answer: Evaluation for a 1.2-litre car: the carburettor is ruled out by emissions. MPFI meets the limits at moderate cost and is robust and easy to service, which suits a price-sensitive small car with a naturally aspirated engine. GDI gives better fuel economy and suits a downsized turbocharged 1.0 to 1.2-litre engine, but adds cost, needs a particulate filter and is more sensitive to fuel quality and deposits.

Recommendation: for a low-cost naturally aspirated 1.2-litre car, MPFI; if the maker uses a turbocharged downsized engine to gain efficiency, GDI with homogeneous operation and a particulate filter. Either way the decision rests on emissions first, then cost against fuel economy.
Check of the reasoning: each claim follows from where and how the fuel is metered: fixed jets (carburettor), pulse at the port (MPFI), pulse in the cylinder (GDI).

bank.q: Explain why a common rail system with split injection can lower both NOx and smoke where an in-line jerk pump cannot, using injection pressure, timing and heat-release reasoning. Use the jerk pump's speed-dependent pressure and the common rail quantity relation Q ∝ t√Δp in your answer, and weigh the cost of the change.
outline: Jerk pump: pressure rises with plunger speed and quantity, so low pressure at low speed and load; timing fixed by cam and helix
Common rail: pressure independent of speed; ECU timing; split injection
Pilot shortens delay, smaller premixed spike: less noise and NOx
High pressure at all speeds: fine spray, less soot; after-injection burns soot
Trade-off and cost
answer: The NOx-soot trade-off: NOx forms where burned gas is hottest (high peak temperature, early combustion); soot forms in fuel-rich zones where fuel and air mix poorly and burns out only if the late cycle is hot and well mixed. Retarding injection lowers NOx but raises soot; raising pressure lowers soot. A system that can control pressure and timing separately, and shape the rate of heat release, can lower both.

Jerk pump limits: injection pressure is made by the plunger moving against the nozzle, so it rises with pump speed and with the fuel quantity. At low speed and light load the pressure is low, the spray is coarse and soot is high. The start of injection is fixed by the cam and helix (with only a mechanical advance), and there is one injection per cycle, so the rate of injection, and the heat release, follow the cam profile.

Ignition delay and the premixed spike: in a single long injection, all fuel injected during the delay period mixes and then burns at once. This premixed burn gives a high rate of pressure rise (diesel knock, noise) and a high peak temperature (NOx).

Common rail pressure: the rail holds 1000 to 2000 bar at any speed, so the spray is fine at idle and low speed as well as at full load: better mixing, less soot. Quantity is set by the open time: Q ∝ t√Δp; for example 30 mm³ takes 1.0 ms at 1200 bar but only 0.81 ms at 1800 bar, so higher pressure also shortens injection and keeps combustion compact.

Pilot injection: a small pilot pulse burns first and heats the charge, so the main fuel ignites with a short delay; little fuel collects before ignition, the premixed spike shrinks, noise and peak temperature fall, and NOx falls.
Main injection timing: the ECU can retard the main pulse slightly to lower NOx further, and recover the soot penalty with the higher pressure and an after-injection.

After and post injection: a small after-injection just after the main keeps the late cycle hot and turbulent and burns soot; a late post injection heats the exhaust to regenerate the particulate filter.

answer.text: Heat-release picture (describe or sketch): a single-injection curve shows a tall early spike followed by a diffusion tail; a pilot-main-after curve shows a small pilot bump, a lower and broader main peak, and a stronger late burn.

answer: Cost of the change: a high-pressure pump, rail, sensors, electronic injectors and ECU cost several times a mechanical pump; fuel must be filtered finely and be free of water; service needs diagnostic equipment; the pump takes more engine power. These are justified where emission limits and noise matter (cars, trucks), and less so on low-cost stationary engines.

Conclusion: the jerk pump couples pressure, quantity and timing to the cam, so it can only trade NOx against soot. Common rail decouples them, and split injection shapes the heat release, so both NOx and soot can be lowered together, at a higher system cost.
Check: √(1140/1740) = 0.809, so 0.81 ms; the logic holds for any pressure pair, since t ∝ 1/√Δp for fixed Q.
